name: Pulmonary Nodules, Screening & Workup
cards: Nodule size that raises suspicion?
Greater than 6 mm.
Spiculated nodule border means?
Spikes, deviations, or lobulations in the border.
Lung locations that make a nodule concerning?
Upper lobes or hilar structures.
Number of nodules that raises concern?
More than 3 nodules.
Change over time that makes a nodule concerning?
Enlarging in size.
Concerning nodule finding on contrast computed tomography?
Contrast enhancement.
Nodule appearances that raise concern besides spiculation?
Cavitated or nonsolid.
Patient factor that makes a nodule more concerning?
High risk of lung cancer.
Benign nodule border?
Well-defined, smooth borders.
Fat inside a lung nodule suggests?
Hamartoma.
Popcorn calcification in a nodule suggests?
Hamartoma.
Smooth nodule with central calcification on computed tomography?
Healed granuloma.
Benign calcification patterns?
Diffuse, central, popcorn, and concentric.
Malignant calcification patterns?
Ground-glass (stippled) and eccentric.
Nodule close to a fissure usually indicates?
Something usually benign.
Nodular opacity beside the minor fissure is typically?
A linear scar or lymphoid tissue.
Lung cancer screening ages?
Adults 55 to 80 years old.
Smoking history required for lung cancer screening?
At least a 30 pack-year history.
Smoking status that qualifies for lung cancer screening?
Currently smokes, or quit within the last 15 years.
Lung cancer screening test and interval?
Low-dose chest computed tomography every year.
Lung cancer screening is only for patients without what?
Symptoms or a known nodule.
Patient with hemoptysis: screening or workup?
Diagnostic workup, not screening.
Why use low-dose computed tomography for screening?
Less radiation than a standard chest computed tomography.
Why can low-dose computed tomography still find nodules?
High contrast between air and lung nodules.
Main upside of lung cancer screening?
Early detection, allowing rapid intervention and a better prognosis.
Main downside of lung cancer screening?
Many false positives leading to unnecessary workups, such as biopsy.
Most common benign lung nodules?
Granuloma (inflammatory) or hamartoma (connective tissue growth).
What is a hamartoma?
A benign connective tissue growth.
Solitary nodule on a chest X-ray is sometimes called?
A coin lesion.
How are most lung nodules found?
Incidentally, on imaging done for another reason.
First evaluation of an incidental nodule?
Estimate its size.
Nodule size generally not concerning unless high risk?
Smaller than 6 mm.
Small nodule in a high-risk patient?
Worked up to exclude malignancy.
Guidelines for follow-up of incidental lung nodules?
Fleischner Society guidelines (updated 2017).
Single solid nodule under 6 mm in a low-risk patient?
No routine follow-up.
Role of the chest X-ray in nodule workup?
Poor tool; may first spot it or rule out other pathology.
Standard imaging for a suspicious nodule?
Contrast computed tomography of the chest and upper abdomen.
How is a lung nodule biopsied?
Bronchoscopy, transthoracic, or thoracoscopic, chosen by location.
How does positron emission tomography flag a malignant nodule?
Highly metabolic cells take up the radioactive sugar.
Low or normal nodule uptake on positron emission tomography?
A good sign.
Why can a glowing nodule on positron emission tomography be benign?
Inflammatory conditions can also take up the sugar.
Sputum cytology for detecting lung cancer?
Not sensitive.
Blood tests in the lung cancer workup?
Complete blood count with differential, metabolic panel with calcium, alkaline phosphatase.
New solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm: first step?
Assess the clinical probability of malignancy.
Very low probability nodule of 8 to 30 mm?
Computed tomography surveillance at 3 to 6, 9 to 12, and 18 to 24 months.
Low to moderate probability nodule of 8 to 30 mm?
Fludeoxyglucose positron emission tomography of the nodule.
Moderate or intense uptake on positron emission tomography?
Nonsurgical biopsy or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection.
High probability nodule with no metastases on staging?
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection.
Who receives a high-probability nodule referral?
Pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist, or oncologist.
Fit for surgery, biopsy confirms malignancy?
Lobectomy.
Fit for surgery but unfit for lobectomy?
Anatomical segmentectomy.
Wedge resection frozen section shows cancer?
Completion lobectomy under the same anesthetic.
Unfit for surgery, malignancy confirmed?
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation, or radical radiotherapy.
Unfit for surgery and biopsy unsafe?
Proceed straight to radiotherapy or ablation.
Biopsy negative but a false negative is feared?
Repeat biopsy or proceed to treatment.

name: Lung Cancer Basics, Presentation & Staging
icon: <path d="M3 20h18"/><rect x="5" y="13" width="3" height="7"/><rect x="10.5" y="9" width="3" height="11"/><rect x="16" y="5" width="3" height="15"/>
cards: Why is lung cancer so deadly?
Symptoms appear only once it is advanced or metastatic.
Share of lung cancers in people under 40?
About 4%, so it stays on the differential.
Lung cancer staging system?
TNM (tumor, node, metastasis).
When is lung cancer staged?
Once computed tomography, positron emission tomography, and biopsy results return.
What computed tomography adds to staging?
Tumor location and size.
What positron emission tomography adds to staging?
Lymph node involvement.
What the biopsy adds to staging?
The tumor type.
Nodes that automatically make stage 3?
N2 or N3 (mediastinal or contralateral nodes).
Metastasis status of all stage 1 to 3 tumors?
M0, no distant metastasis.
T1 tumor size?
3 cm or less.
T2 tumor size?
More than 3 cm, up to 5 cm.
T3 tumor size?
More than 5 cm, up to 7 cm.
T4 tumor size?
More than 7 cm.
N1 lymph nodes?
Same-side peribronchial, hilar, or intrapulmonary nodes.
N2 lymph nodes?
Same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes.
N3 lymph nodes?
Opposite-side mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular node.
M1a spread?
Opposite lung, pleural or pericardial nodule, or malignant effusion.
M1b spread?
A single metastasis outside the chest.
M1c spread?
Multiple metastases outside the chest.
Stage 1A?
Tumor 3 cm or less, no lymph node spread.
Stage 1B?
Tumor more than 3 cm up to 4 cm, no nodes.
Stage 2A?
Tumor more than 4 cm up to 5 cm, no nodes.
Tumor 5 cm or less with peribronchial or hilar nodes?
Stage 2B.
Tumor 5 cm or less with mediastinal nodes?
Stage 3A.
Tumor 5 cm or less with a supraclavicular node?
Stage 3B.
Tumor over 5 cm with opposite-side or supraclavicular nodes?
Stage 3C.
Spread to the other lung, or one site outside the chest?
Stage 4A.
Spread to multiple sites outside the chest?
Stage 4B.
Lung cancer share of cancer deaths in men?
More than 30%: the highest of all cancers in men.
Lung cancer five-year survival in the United States?
About 17 to 18%.
Share of lung cancers in which smoking is implicated?
Share of lung cancer from second-hand smoke?
About 20%.
Effect of packs per day and years of smoking?
They compound the risk: 5x to 10x to 20x.
Environmental lung cancer risks besides smoking?
Radiation and radon, air pollution, environmental and chemical toxins.
Infections that raise lung cancer risk?
Tuberculosis or human immunodeficiency virus infection.
New lung cancer cases each year in the United States?
More than 200,000.
Age group with most lung cancers?
People over 50 years old.
Two main types of lung carcinoma?
Small cell and non-small cell.
Small cell share of lung cancers?
Other name for small cell carcinoma?
Oat cell carcinoma.
Three non-small cell subtypes?
Adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma.
Rare lung cancer types?
Carcinoid, bronchial gland, sarcomatoid, and Pancoast tumors.
Cells that lung carcinomas arise from?
Epithelial cells.
How carcinogens cause lung cancer?
Activate oncogenes and inactivate tumor-suppressing genes.
Distant organs lung cancer spreads to?
Liver, brain, and bone.
Lung cancer growth sequence?
Hyperplasia, dysplasia, in situ cancer, invasive tumor, metastases.
Type I pneumocyte job?
Gas exchange over about 95% of the alveolar surface.
Type II pneumocyte job?
Secretes pulmonary surfactant.
Share of alveolar cells that are type II pneumocytes?
About 60%, but only 3 to 5% of the surface.
Respiratory symptoms that prompt a lung cancer workup?
Persistent cough, hemoptysis, dysphagia, wheezing, shortness of breath.
Systemic symptoms that prompt a lung cancer workup?
Weight loss, fever, fatigue, bone or chest pain, endocrine disorders.
Brain metastasis symptoms?
Headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncope, seizures.
Brain metastasis sign of raised intracranial pressure?
Papilledema on fundoscopic exam.
Liver metastasis findings?
Dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, jaundice.
Bone metastasis warning sign?
Fractures without falls, even from a cough.
Adrenal metastasis electrolytes?
Hyponatremia with hyperkalemia.
Adrenal insufficiency symptoms from metastasis?
Fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension.

name: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
cards: Which two lung cancers are central?
Small cell and squamous cell carcinoma.
Which two lung cancers are peripheral?
Adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma.
Memory aid for the central lung cancers?
Small and squamous are central: the two S types.
Unusual metastatic site specific to large cell carcinoma?
Small intestine and bowel.
Lung cancer with the strongest smoking association?
Squamous cell carcinoma.
Squamous cell carcinoma location?
Central, often arising in a bronchus.
Squamous cell symptoms once it obstructs a bronchus?
Cough, wheezing, and hemoptysis.
Lung cancer that sputum cytology can catch?
Squamous cell carcinoma.
Paraneoplastic syndrome particularly tied to squamous cell?
Hypercalcemia.
Non-small cell stage 1 to 2 treatment?
Surgical resection.
Non-small cell stage 4 treatment?
Chemotherapy.
Stage 4 non-small cell: when is surgery used?
Solitary metastasis with a resectable primary tumor.
Squamous cell share of lung cancers?
20 to 30%, the second most common.
Squamous cell course before obstruction?
Asymptomatic until it obstructs the bronchus.
Large bronchial obstruction from squamous cell leads to?
Atelectasis and pneumonia risk.
Squamous cell local invasion signs?
Dysphagia and voice changes (laryngeal nerves).
Squamous cell nodal spread?
Lymphangitic spread to the hilar lymph nodes.
Squamous cell carcinoma on computed tomography?
Large cavitated spiculated lesion with nodular inner margins.
Squamous cell structural features?
Frequent cavitation and obstruction.
Most common lung cancer?
Adenocarcinoma.
Usual cell of origin of adenocarcinoma?
Type II pneumocytes.
Precursor lesion of adenocarcinoma?
Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia.
Lepidic growth?
Tumor growth across the alveolar lining.
Adenocarcinoma location?
Mid-lung and periphery.
Adenocarcinoma and scars?
Frequently associated with peripheral scars.
Adenocarcinoma first spread?
To the lymphatics, before leaving the lungs.
Stain showing mucin in adenocarcinoma?
Mucicarmine stain.
Negative mucicarmine stain may point to?
Large cell carcinoma.
Share of adenocarcinomas found advanced or metastatic?
About two-thirds.
Later signs of adenocarcinoma?
Bone pain, weight loss, paraneoplastic issues.
Adenocarcinoma and smoking?
Usually smokers, but smoking is not always involved.
Adenocarcinoma cough pattern?
Persistent cough and dyspnea without signs of infection.
Peripheral spiculated nodule involving the pleura proved to be?
Invasive adenocarcinoma.
Adenocarcinoma invasion categories?
Noninvasive, minimally invasive, or invasive.
Large cell carcinoma is a diagnosis of?
Exclusion: no specific genetic or histologic markers.
Large cell carcinoma histology?
Anaplastic, undifferentiated, pleomorphic cells.
Large cell carcinoma cell size?
About 3 times larger than baseline cells.
Large cell carcinoma location?
Periphery.
Large cell carcinoma on computed tomography?
Large, cavitated peripheral mass.
Large cell tendency versus other non-small cell types?
Necrosis and hemorrhage more readily.
Large cell carcinoma treatment?
No standardized treatment, due to variety and rarity.
Large cell share of lung cancers?
Why is large cell kept apart from small cell?
Their treatments differ.
Large cell carcinoma confirmation?
Biopsy with histology showing anaplastic tissue.
Role of chemotherapy and radiation in non-small cell cancer?
Adjuncts to surgery, or for stage 4.
Why chemotherapy and radiation are only adjuncts in non-small cell?
Non-small cell cancers respond poorly to them.
Requirement before lung cancer resection?
Patient can tolerate surgery: survive and recover.
Wedge resection removes?
A small portion of a lobe.
Segment resection removes?
A larger portion of a lobe.
Lobectomy removes?
An entire lobe.
Pneumonectomy removes?
An entire lung.
Purpose of tumor genetic testing?
Lets the oncologist tailor therapy.
TP53 (tumor protein 53) role?
Tumor-suppressor gene; damage lets cancer grow.
Immunotherapy drugs ending in -mab?
Monoclonal antibodies, such as checkpoint inhibitors.
How checkpoint inhibitors work?
Block tumor cells from switching off T cells.
Gene-marker targeted therapy is for which non-small cell types?
Non-squamous types; squamous cell is excluded.
Mixed lung carcinoma types?
Adenosquamous or combined small cell carcinoma.

name: Small Cell Lung Cancer & Paraneoplastic Syndromes
cards: Lung cancer that benefits most from radiotherapy?
Small cell lung carcinoma.
Small cell response to chemotherapy and radiation?
Better than the three non-small cell types.
Small cell stage in which radiation works best?
Limited stage.
Purpose of prophylactic cranial irradiation?
Treat the brain because brain metastasis is so likely.
Limited-stage small cell after a complete or partial response?
Prophylactic cranial irradiation.
Extensive-stage small cell after a response?
Consider cranial irradiation, with or without thoracic radiotherapy.
Lung cancer type that typically causes paraneoplastic syndromes?
Small cell lung carcinoma.
Cells lining the bronchioles behind paraneoplastic syndromes?
Neuroendocrine cells.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone comes from which lung cancer?
Small cell lung cancer.
Hormone in excess in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone?
Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin).
Sodium and osmolality in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone?
Hyponatremia and decreased serum osmolality.
Neurologic signs of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone?
Confusion, seizures, ataxia.
Edema in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone?
None, peripheral or pulmonary; it develops insidiously.
Low sodium with high potassium and hypotension suggests?
Adrenal insufficiency from a metastasis.
Small cell carcinoma location?
Central; infiltrates the mucosa.
Share of small cell cancers metastatic before detection?
Over 70%.
Common small cell metastatic sites?
Liver, bone, and brain.
Small cell confined to one area with local nodes?
Limited stage.
Small cell spread beyond the local area?
Extensive stage.
Combined small cell carcinoma?
Mixed with non-small cell histology.
Small cell histology?
Small cells, no nucleoli, high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio.
Why is small cell often crushed at biopsy?
It is a fragile tumor.
Small cell genetic association?
Lesion of the short arm of chromosome 3.
Immunotherapy in small cell?
Less effective from genetic variability, but becoming an option.
Small cell cavitation?
High cavitation rate once large enough for symptoms.
Cells that small cell paraneoplastic symptoms can arise from?
APUD (amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation) cells.
Cranial irradiation is not recommended with?
Poor performance status or impaired neurocognitive function.
Preferred brain imaging before cranial irradiation?
Magnetic resonance imaging rather than computed tomography.
How a linear accelerator limits whole-body radiation?
Beams focus on the targeted area.
Acute skin effects of radiotherapy?
Erythema, hyperpigmentation, and ulceration risk.
Nausea with radiotherapy compared with chemotherapy?
Limited; radiotherapy is less systemic.
Chronic lung effect of chest radiotherapy?
Pulmonary fibrosis and scarring.
Chronic heart effects of chest radiotherapy?
Coronary artery disease, valve disease, cardiomyopathy.
Effect of radiotherapy damage to lymphatics?
Lymphedema and fluid retention.
Chronic nerve effect of radiotherapy?
Neuropathy.
Cause of paraneoplastic syndromes?
Hormonal or cytokine effects of tumor tissue.
Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes of lung cancer?
SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone) and hypercalcemia.
Lab panel that checks calcium in the lung cancer workup?
Comprehensive metabolic panel including calcium.
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome target?
Calcium channels on nerve endings.
Lambert-Eaton effect at the neuromuscular junction?
Too little acetylcholine released.
Lambert-Eaton weakness pattern?
Progressive weakness, particularly in the legs.
Neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes of lung cancer?
Lambert-Eaton syndrome, cerebellar degeneration, encephalitis.
Dermatologic paraneoplastic syndromes of lung cancer?
Acanthosis nigricans or dermatomyositis.
Lung source of carcinoid syndrome?
A bronchial carcinoid tumor.
Hormone released in carcinoid syndrome?
Serotonin.
Carcinoid syndrome skin findings?
Cutaneous flushes and apparent cyanosis.
Carcinoid syndrome heart findings?
Pulmonic and tricuspid valve thickening and stenosis.
Carcinoid syndrome gastrointestinal findings?
Diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting.
Carcinoid syndrome respiratory findings?
Cough, wheezing, dyspnea.
Carcinoid syndrome fibrosis sites?
Endocardial, retroperitoneal, and pelvic fibrosis.
